hiring manager and ask me questions/etc etc". 4. when you get to the phone screening, think of it as the telephone game. you have to have your elevator pitch simple enough for the recruiter to Name: 0_cs_just_like_students
Representative_Docs: ["update: hope scholarship getting bumped to 100% tuition for fiscal year 2024! keeping hope or zell isn't the only incentive to perform academically. i'd assume most students want to get a job after graduation or get accepted into a good grad school. higher academic performance helps provide better pickings for both. same goes for the high school level. do you just want to do good enough to get hope, or do you want to have the academic credentials to get into a school like tech? back in my day at the high school i went to, you had to take multiple ap and dual enrollment level classes to get into tech, but the challenge of those classes disqualified some of us who got into tech from zell (we still maintained hope). some students didn't bother taking those advanced classes for risk of losing zell but would if it wouldn't affect their financial ability to afford college in the first place", 'transfer advice. thinking about changing schools. again. hey y’all, i need some advice. i’m a new transfer student from out of state. to be honest, it’s been a rough few weeks. gt has always been my dream school and i thought this would be the place i’d finally settle down, but since coming here, it’s been really hard to find my place. i met a few people in my faset group, but we’re all different majors and some of them commute so we’re not super close. i tried informal rush but got dropped by every sorority. however, i’m mostly concerned about the competitive culture. i knew it would difficult, but i’d heard my classes would be more collaborative than i’ve experienced them to be. i’ve found it very hard to do group work or ask for help in my classes. i’ll reach out to my group with questions about lecture or hw and they will either not respond or say they didn’t see my message until after the hw/exam passes. i’m fine with going to oh, but i feel some questions don’t need to be directly answered by the professor when a simple text can suffice. at my old school my friends and i would study together and help each other as much as possible. i just thought that was the norm. i get the vibe that students here think helping others is in some way disadvantaging them. so i ask…does it get better? is this just typical of intro courses and people will warm up over time? i’m seriously contemplating switching schools again. i’m tired and just want to be settled in somewhere. app deadlines are coming up and i need to figure out what to do. what are y’all’s thoughts? any advice is appreciated. thanks!', 'cs course access: what has been done and why it\'s still difficult for you. in the deepest recesses of the internet, irate students post this stuff: "why am i only registered for one course and waitlisted for eight?? the cs department wants us to stay here forever so they can suck the money out of our pockets because they are evil crooks. why can\'t they wave a magic wand and make more sections appear out of thin air?? i\'m gonna ~~spam~~ email the professo burdell until they fix this shit!! but first i\'m gonna ragepost on that will show \'em!!!" (420 upvotes, gilded 10x, reddit silver 5x) hot "takes" like the above are not completely true and i\'m setting the record straight. almost everything here is factual and backed by sources. ​ over the years, there have been changes that ease registration and access for computing students, sometimes to the chagrin of others. cs courses have major restrictions so computing students can get into them. this was not always the case. in fall 2012 the coc employed [2 advisors]( kathy and cathy. that had grown to [7 by 2016]( [they now employ 15]( advisors. i have seen people complain about their advisor changing. advisors often change because the workload has to be redistributed when someone new is hired. double majors are heavily restricted in the coc because you had students who would declare a double major just to take a few courses and then drop it, shutting cs majors out of courses they need to graduate. thread restrictions are annoying, but they exist so students in those threads can get into classes they need. thread restrictions were not a thing in \\~2016-17. at one point, ml was [only offered in spring]( and cv was only in fall. now both are offered in the fall, spring, and sometimes summer, and this is also true for other courses (3630, 3790, 4210, 4460, 4660,...) the college of computing hires new faculty every year. remember, the coc is made up of five schools which all hire each year (i.e. this list is nowhere near exhaustive) [fall 2019]( \\- school of cse - 3 new hires [fall 2020]( \\- school of ic - 7 new hires [fall 2021]( \\- computing wide - 11 new tt hires, 3 lecture track [fall 2022]( \\- school of cse - 4 new hires fall 2023 - offers have been accepted and we will meet the new professors soon. with new faculty comes increased capacity in courses. shown is a table of popular courses and available seats over time. source: oscar. ||fall 2013|fall 2016|fall 2019|fall 2022| |:-|:-|:-|:-|:-| |cs majors (per lite)|1,192|2,046|2,696|4,234| |cs 1331|400|644|915|1,058| |cs 1332|300|500|567|1,140| |cs 2340|175|432|462|635| |cs 3251|60|200|138 \\|270| |cs 3451|100|106|150|250| |cs 3600|75|276|487|344 (explained [here]( |cs 4641|80 \\\\|110|385|485| \\ - idk what happened here. fall 2018 and spring 2020 had more students. \\\\ - spring 2014, it was not offered in fall 2013. not every course has scaled perfectly (3600/4641 sure haven\'t), but they are not ignoring demand. "if there are 200 people on the waitlist for cs xxxx, can\'t they just make another section??" faculty teaching assignments are planned ahead of time. if they make a new section of an undergraduate course in the middle of registration, who would teach it? you could get a very senior phd student, but good luck finding one who\'s willing. where would this new section be taught? there aren\'t many large lecture halls on campus, and their dockets are full. you could have an online section, but the professor has to be willing to teach it, and some aren\'t. i\'d bet the online sections we see this semester are taught by professors who agreed to it ahead of time. tas are another issue. [the coc typically employs 1 ta for every 25 students]( in lower division classes (ctrl+f 25). if a new section of cs xxxx with 200 seats appears a week before the term starts, 8 tas must be hired. i\'d hate to be the professor who has this new section dropped on them and has to hire a bunch of tas. "why can\'t the stupid lazy useless advisors get me into an existing section??" first off, [advisors are not lazy, stupid, nor useless]( if you are a graduating senior (oag filled out), they will bump you to the top of the waitlist for a class you need if you email them. they don\'t do it automatically because students often have multiple choices for classes to fulfill a requirement and advisors can\'t read your minds. if you\'re not graduating, they typically won\'t pull any strings because what\'s done for you must be done for all and space is limited. "but other schools don\'t have these issues!! georgia tech is the only university in the world with problems because other places care about their students!!!" this is not true. read the complaints for yourself... uc berkeley - [\\[1\\]]( [\\[2\\]]( [\\[3\\]]( ut austin - [\\[1\\]]( [\\[2\\]]( other places - [georgia state]( [u of maryland]( [ut dallas]( [boston u]( [uw madison]( [purdue]( i\'ve seen people insist that gt should take a heavy-handed approach and start dramatically cutting cs enrollment. as the berkeley and ut austin links show, having restrictions doesn\'t erase problems. doing this also introduces some access/equity issues that i can expand on if someone wants. at many peer universities, especially public peers, cs is locked down. do you really want to attend a university where you [compete]( with [your peers]( for spots in [the major]( how about a place where cs is [off]( limits [to]( you [altogether]( in a landscape where cs programs everywhere are getting restricted, it is not a bad thing that georgia tech has chosen not to follow its peers. i was going to offer a list of things that the coc and other units can do to mitigate capacity issues, but this post is long enough. that will come in my [next thread]( ​ tl;dr: the college of computing is well aware of space and capacity issues in courses and they have done a lot to mitigate these problems. they\'ve hired faculty, increased space in courses, offered key thread picks more often, and a host of other things. the coc prioritizes graduating students on waitlists, and advisors will not always bend over backward for you for many reasons, but it doesn\'t mean they don\'t care. overcrowding in cs programs is a problem at many universities right now.']

Name: 4_bike_parking_bus_scooter
Representative_Docs: ['is bike theft common? is it ok to bring my somewhat expensive road bike? just bring a cheap bike to campus and don’t stress about it. you’ll have enough to worry about.', "ferst dr. - 6th st. intersection rework just wanted to a have a discussion about the feasibility of making the ferst. dr. - 6th st. intersection -- the intersection down the hill from the crc, nearby the west residence halls, the burger bowl, the love building, etc. -- both safer and more efficient at reducing traffic for all: drivers, bikers/scooters, and pedestrians. the current infrastructure for this intersection has pretty large signs on each side of the intersection that flash when a pedestrian or light vehicle presses a button, warning the drivers. as these signs don't actually moderate flow like stop signs or lights, they just warn, there are also stop signs. however the characteristics of this intersection create an interesting right-of-way pattern: you can't call it a 4-way stop, even though it has 4 perpendicular directions of motion for each mode of transportation. to the driver, it's a 2-way, there's only going straight, or turning west; its not a 3-way since 6th street here is one-way; it's not a 4-way since cars can't travel east onto the sidewalk that leads to boggs and on to the culc. to the light vehicle (again, bikes and scooters), its legally a 4-way -- east towards culc, north, south towards crc, and west towards the residence halls, each direction having stop signs. but only as of recently have these stop signs actually been obeyed, as countless times i witness (and i'm guilty as well a few times), light vehicles just blasting through the stop signs. i have seen a reddit post somewhere on this subreddit from gtpd saying they were going to crackdown on this disobeying. i have seen on multiple occasions a cop car sitting on the sidewalk waiting to spot someone. to the pedestrian, the stop sign isn't present, as the pedestrian (unless there's a walk/no walk sign) always has the right of way at intersections ​ just from observing the intersection at rush hour, its just obviously inefficient. what i witness is a car staying at a stop sign for 20 or 30 seconds or more because as the car rolls up to the stop sign, a pedestrian from the right side starts to cross . . . then as p#1 is almost done crossing, p#2 from the left starts to cross . . . then a bike from the right goes right through the stop sign . . . and then the road is clear to continue. this amount of time compounds greatly during rush hour to create a line of cars that sometimes goes up to the crc. do i have a definitive solution? no, for multiple reasons, not being an expert in city planning being one of them. do i have an idea or suggestion that i feel like could be discussed. yes! thats why i made this post :) those who frequent the bioengineering center or the nanotechnology center know that at the intersection between atlantic dr. nw and ferst dr. has a light, but not only does it have a light for cars, but also a light for bicycles. having a light between the light vehicles/pedestrians and the cars would coordinate the motion between the two groups, thereby improving the speed and safety of each. ​ what do you guys think? could something similar be implemented at 6th street? for economic reasons should it be? is it even needed in the first place or is the intersection fine as it is?", "bikes on stinger buses, bike racks? no bike racks (except maybe on the emory shuttle) and i've never seen anyone bring a bike onto a gt bus. gt campus is not so large that if you have a bike, you should need to bring it on to a bus rather than just riding it."]
